newsitem.title: FRANCE: French franc rise puts rate cut on agenda - RPT.
newsitem.headline: French franc rise puts rate cut on agenda - RPT.

text.p: The steady rise in the franc against the mark to near four-year highs has given the Bank of France room to cut its key intervention rate although only a minority of analysts expect a move this week.

Two-thirds of economists polled by Reuters forecast the central bank would leave the intervention rate, which sets the floor for money market rates, unchanged at 3.10 percent after a regular monetary policy council meeting on Thursday.
However, a growing number of economists believe the Bank of France will move soon to narrow the gap between French and German money market rates to five basis points from 10.
The gap between French and German official money market rates, set by central banks, is wider than at any other point along the French yield curve.

Some analysts said there was little reason to keep the differential as protection against a weaker currency given the franc's strength and that sluggish economic growth and a benign inflation outlook still argued in favour of cuts.
The franc broke through 3.37 on March 27 and climbed as high as 3.3627 against the mark on Tuesday, its highest level since June 1993. Both 10- and 20-day moving averages moved below 3.37.

Analysts and traders said there was a widespread view that the French central bank had been selling the franc between 3.3700 and 3.3710 to stop it climbing too quickly to its central parity in the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) at 3.3538.

"Historically there have been two good hints of forthcoming rate cuts. One is the direction of franc - when its appreciating they usually cut rates - and second if they lower call money they cut rates," Marie Owens-Thomsen, economist at BIP, said.
"Since autumn the Bank of France has been defending 3.37 and suddenly it stopped defending it. Why has it changed its behaviour if it doesn't have a reason?" she said.

Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet has said on numerous occasions he thinks the franc should enter a single European currency at its central rate and analysts said the central bank would prefer gradual appreciation during the course of the next two years.
Jean-Francois Mercier, economist at Salomon Brothers, said the fact the Bank of France had appeared to let the franc rise past 3.37 did not necessarily mean rates would be cut.
"At the margin I expect rates to remain unchanged, although I wouldn't be overly surprised if there were a cut given the rise in the franc" which has given it more latitude, he said.

"That said we've had no sign they're intending to change the call money rate and in recent speeches there's been nothing to suggest they may change their stance. It could just be the Bank of France wants the franc to move back (to its central rate) gradually," Mercier said.

While a five basis point cut would have little tangible effect on economic growth, some said it could lower bond yields if it were seen as a symbolic gesture to reinforce the view that European interest rates will stay for low for some time even if growth picks up this year.

"The Bank of France, and no doubt the Bundesbank, are worried by rise of European bond yields. One of their tasks is to convince markets there is no rate rise to fear in France or Germany and that if they move it will be down," Antoine Brunet, economist at Credit Commercial de France, said.
"If the Bank of France does something Thursday, it would be a gesture that there's no fear of a German rate rise before the end of year," he said.

Brunet was more sceptical about the likelihood the Bank of France would cut rates to weaken the franc and said it would be more likely to continue a policy of discreet intervention to manage any move higher.
Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst, said he did not think the franc would become a major issue for the Bank of France unless it were to go through its central parity in the ERM.

"Fundamentally the franc has room to keep progressively strengthening against the mark. I think Trichet would certainly be very concerned if it breaks through the parity but now its in a comfortable range for the Bank of France," he said.
